The scourge that has been prostrating our
horses for the past six weeks in the shape Of
influenza is now assuming more fatal charac-
ter in the form Of dropsy, and in some stables
farcy and glanders have followed the epizootic
symptoms. There is no question but that
private horses have been more free from the
disease than those that have been overworked
on railroads, stages and carts; but those who
have had palaces for homes have not been
exempt from the plague and have had all the
various stages of the disease to the last and
fatal one of dropsy. Veterinary science has
been all abroad about the diagnosis Of the
scourge Mr.. Dunbar does not believe that the
disease was atmospherically infectious, while
Professor Taylor declares that it is contagious,
diseased horses away from well ones. It was
argued by some scientific gentlemen when the
disease first broke out that there was no
danger whatever, except relapse by exposure, to
the well-conditioned horse; but we have seen
during the last few days that the reverse is the
case, and dropsy, farcy and glanders are now
ending the miseries of many horses that were
receiving the greatest care and were supposed
to be improving week ago. We hope that we
have seen the worst of this horse disease, and
that the clear atmosphere which we are now
enjoying may stay the ravages of the scourge
in our stables and that the debiltated animals
may recuperate rapidly; but we advise care in
keeping the diseased animals away from the
well ones, and where farcy or glanders is dis
covered to destroy the horse at once.

Emigration from Alsace and Lorraine.


The conquered provinces of France do not
take kindly to German rule. Homes Of long
years standing are broken up and those who
inhabited them are leaving for foreign parts.
Unlike the Germans, the French are not great
colonizers. Even in this country, where in
ducements are numerous to emigrants and
where wealth and reward invite the active
and ambitious, we have had comparatively
small number of emigrants from France.
When the war closed in France, and the
German troops, with the exception of the
army of occupation, vacated the French prov
inces, the Alsatians and Lorrainians displayed
a FESTIVE disposition and dislike to live under
German rule. Emigration followed and has
since continued. The population of Metz has
already been diminished by over one-third.
About fifteen hundred of the inhabitants of the
two provinces sought Algeria as their future
home and refuge, but their destitute condition
untitled them for the colony they sought
TO establish. America is now the land
which attracts the French emigrants, and
Canada, rather than the United States, the
particular location on the Continent. 1t
is estimated that over seventeen thousand have
already gone to Canada, and more are sure to
follow. Among those coming across the At
lantic are skilled mechanics and artisans, o
class of people who will find the United States
a much more profitable field for their energy
than the Canadas, and We doubt not that some
of these, at least, will direct their course to


the Great Republic,

The infamous outrage that the Democratic
leaders have perpetrsted upon their constit-
uency in proclaiming in advance false Demo-
cratic victory in North Carolina has caused
such universal ridicule as to make the leaders
objects Of contempt in the eyes of thousands
of honest Democrats throughout the land. In
every city and town over the national domain
Democratic powder was expended to give ad-
ditional jolliication to the occasion. Demo-
Gratis yelled themselves hoarse, laughed them
selves weary and exhausted all of their crow
ing propensities in exulting our Republicans
for losing the State. When the real fact became
known those who had been unjustly made the
victims felt kindling of wrath in their breasts.
The amusement for Republicans was doubly
augmented by the many extravaganzas that
were recklessly gotten off by Democratic over.
flowing Joy at what they were told was the
dawn of that "good time coming" whom the
''lost cause" should be regained.


In every town, village, hamlet and farm
house wherever postoffice or newspaper is
known to throw ray of intelligence, one uni
versal contempt and condemnation goes up
from the heart Of the honest Democrat for those
who have m ade him their dupe for obvious rea-
ons,while theloud and exultantlaugh rings out
heartily and clear from Republicans and all
those who havea good appreciation ofthe redic-
ulous. Before folks were through with the
happy errand of carrying "the news to Hiram"
they discovered that they were not exactly the
folks to bear so inn portant message. The music
Of the wires flashed the glad tidings of $4,000
Democratic majority for North Carolina all
over the country. In twinkling Democrats
everywhere stopped their work, laid down
their pipes, abandoned whatever they had in
hand and betook themselves to philosophy and
figures, the rising and setting of the ''tidal
wave" in the direction of . Democratic national
triumph, speculating upon the arrival of the
long wished and earnestly prayed form Demo-
cratic worship-something "to beat Grant"
Liberal Republican Democrats hugged their
wives, kissed their babies and congratulated
their families, that Horace was drifting towards
the White House.


But before the joy that was boundless had
time to subside and die away it was nipped by
the cruel intelligence that the whole affair was
false alarm perpetrated by Democratic in
clination to make Democrats feel good after an
election. This was well done, because it was
done at the only time that it could have pro-
duced political happiness in Democratic heart.
Democrats who are capable of it are chagrined.
Fence men exercise an amusing reticence.
Liberal Republicans who have not yet chosen
their company stand upon their dignity and
wisely refuse to make "new acquaintances."


We have no doubt that the Democrats are
well supplied with powder and gas and unless
they begin early and use every occasion they
will not have opportunities enough to get rid
of them by November. Wewould advise them
to use them all up on the state elections for
after the November blast blows upon them
they will reluctantly crawl into their holes and
pull their holes in after them.

COPENHAGEN, Nov. %, 1872.
The recent gale has caused such immense suffer-
ing and calamities that even the Oldest among US
don't remember ANYTHING similar.


SCENE OF DEsoLATIoN ON SHORE.
It is known that some two hundred vessels OF all
sizes have run on shore; but in the bay OF Kjo'ge,
on the east side OF Seeland we see some fifty
crushed ships, deserted by their crews; some OF
the vessels have been thrown more than one thou
sand feet up in the land by the champion waves.
which put several square miles OF that unhappy
town and country under water. All the coasts
turned towards the southeast have been horribly
damaged.


Many lives have been lost, the cattle killed, the
crop spoiled the houses rhined, the wealthy peo-
pie turned poor, the poor people envying the hap
pier dead.


Such is the result OF that terrible night OF the 18th
Of November

1t would be rather difficult to state which is the
worse-the calamity itself or the consequences OF
it--f0r many thousand families who but few
days ago enjoyed gratefully the humble fruits Of
their manful work by day and night stand now
helpless-almost naked-in the unmerciful cold
Winter, looking out for assistance from their fel-
low citizens, who, even doing their best can only
partly succor the sufferers.

6s


Should appoint any class for whom the inun-
dation has been an overwhelming calamity think
deprived them Of their tools, the. waves crushed
their boats and buried their houses, and many OF
those brave ave, men, ne supporters I Of families found

different points the waves were thrown several
miles up In the lowlands, and the unhappy popu-
lation OF the farms and villages started up in the
. dark night, seeing the wild sea, whose far noise
for the threatened sailors, carrying away all

The southern part OF the island, Falsten, has
doubtless sunered most The village OF Botoe and
the surrounding country are still under water, and
are supposed to have disappeared forever The
population here was drowned with all their prop
erty, very few escaping, and that in wonderful
manner.

has lost some nifty lives being about two and half

had ten houses carried away and many others left
waves, and are now deserted by the former inhabi-

are sunk six large vessels and some twenty ran on

At ROdbye, on the island Lolland, was q small

THE CHARITY WHICH CONSOLES AND COMFORTS.
Although the whole country may be said to have
been struck hard by the calamity, all who have
the means stand ready to relieve their unhappy
fellow citizens. All the Danes feel that help must
be rendered Immediately; tnen the extension OF
the calamity cannot even now be seen. And,
truthiully they go ahead with their strong work.
His Majesty King Christian heads the committee
appointed for collecting money for the relief OF the

There comes time when we grow old,
And like sunset down the sea.
Slope gradual, and the night winds cold
Come whispering sad and chillingly;

And eyes of saddest blue behold

There comes time when we grow old.
There comes time when joyous hearts,
Which leaped as leaps the laughing main,
Are dead to all save memory,
A prisoner in his dungeon chain !;

hear voice in whisper say,

That kindled youth to hues Of gold
Still burns with clear and steady ray,
And fond affections, lingering, say,
There comes time when we grow old.
There comes a time when laughing spring
And golden summer cease to be,

To tread the last declivity;

With rosy Hope,
Beyond the sunset we behold
Another dawn with fairer light,

ST. PAUL, Minn., Nov. %, 1872.
At the time the recent terrific wind and snow
storm swept over the Northwest the Winona and
st. Peter Railroad Company was actually pushing
the work along the line Of their road between New
Ulm, which is about one hundred and five miles
west OF st. Paul, in Brown county, Minnesota, and
Lake Campeska in Dakota. Some eight hundred
men and five locomotives were employed. The
storm struck the line OF road on Monday, Novem-
ber II, the men and teams being In temporary shan.
ties and tents, and in consequence of the fine
weather preceding the storm


NO PROVISION HAD BEEN MADE
either In the way OF Iuel or clothing for the sud-
den and severe change in the temperature AS
they were receiving their supplies and provisions
In limited quantities just as required, the storm
caught them totally unprepared to Withstand the
prOtracted siege they were compelled to undergo
before relief eventually reached them. The storm
lasted for about five days, and the snow fell in such
quantities and was so drifted that the entire party
were completely cut of from all communication
with the world.


THE EIGHT HUNDRED MEN


were working in gangs at different points along
the line, but the depth of the snow prevented
them from communicating with each other where
any considerable distance intervened. Nothing
having been heard from this snowed-in party from
Monday the 11th, till Friday, the 18th inst Super
lntendent Stewartand Colonel Degraf determined
to attempt their rescue. Accordingly, last Fri
day, the 18th, they started with five cars and two
locomotives and about one hundred and fifty men
for the purpose Of digging their way to the


sNowED-UP woRKMEN.


The resCuing party were absent six or seven days,
during which time the most exaggerated rumors
OF the sufferings OF the snow-bound workmen were
anoat, and the long absence OF the party who had
gone to their rescue caused great uneasiness. The
oh nj
nothing but the most energetic and untiring work
under the two gentlemen named has prevented
intense suffering and the record of a fearful ca
lamity on the border. Day after day they have
struggled through the drifts and storms, and after
noSsmall amount Of personal suffering and hord-
ship finally succeeded in bringing the men safely
out from the


PERILs OF THE WILDERNESS.


On the return trip three engines and four fat
cars were precipitated through treste bridge at
point seven miles west of Marshall. Two engi-
ncers and a conductor were injured, but their
wounds are not serious. The rescued men, who
have undergone great suffering, arrived at New
Uin last night, where they will remain until they
recover from the effects OF the frontier storm they
have gone through


ANOTHER PARTY OvERTAKEN AND HEMMED IN.


On Monday, the 11th inst, the President and
Directors OF the ST. Paul and Sioux City started
on tour OF inspection over the line. They reached
the Missouri terminus all right, and started on
their return. They were soon overtaken by storm
and showed in. For some eight or ten days nothing
was heard from them, and serious fears for their
safety were entertained by their friends. After a
very rough time, however, the party succeeded in
getting back to st. Paul. considerably the worse lor
their experience of q frontier storm.


The detention OF these two parties has led to SEN
sational reports being sent abroad but really there
has been no serious danger.

with it the bright aud bracing weather which
callers hoped for. The dEizzliny rain, which al
